description: Our project, HimaRakshak AI, aims to leverage NASA Earth observation data, satellite imagery, and Artificial Intelligence to monitor environmental changes and assess potential disaster exposure across Nepal's Himalayan and river-basin regions. Our goal is to transform complex satellite data into meaningful, actionable environmental insights that can support disaster preparedness and help communities better understand the changing environment around them. Our team is interested in AI/ML, DL
summary: HimaRakshak AI transforms climate trend maps into a claim-checking tool for Nepal’s Koshi River Basin through a reproducible Python pipeline and public website that tests eight common climate claims, such as “the monsoon is weakening” and “winters are warmer,” using 24 years (2001–2024) of NASA’s GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, and GRACE/GRACE-FO records, cross-examined against the 2014 satellite change and compared with Nepal’s BIPAD flood reports and Copernicus GloFAS river discharge. Each claim receives one of five fixed verdicts, including “we can’t tell.” Rather than relying on alarming maps, the system prioritizes evidence and reliability: although 44 of 813 grid cells show significant drying trends, only one survives every reliability check, while the two NASA rainfall records disagree on direction, suggesting that much of the apparent drying signal is unreliable. In contrast, autumn warming of +0.19 °C per decade since 1980 passes every check. The platform allows visitors to search for their villages, trace every number to its source file and processing step, and explore how verdicts change across different years. Since rainfall alone preceded only 12% of reported floods, HimaRakshak AI deliberately avoids issuing forecasts or warnings, focusing instead on transparent, reproducible, and evidence-based climate claim verification.
details:
Writing

HimaRakshak AI, meaning “Guardian of the Himalayas,” is a climate claim-checking project designed to find out which climate change claims about Nepal’s Koshi River Basin are actually supported by scientific evidence. It studies the entire transboundary basin, covering 89,251 km² from the Terai plains to the Tibetan Plateau, using 24 years of climate data (2001–2024) and a long-term temperature record from 1980–2024. The project has two main parts: a Python-based data processing pipeline and a public website. The Python pipeline collects climate data from NASA and other trusted sources, downloads only the data needed for the Koshi Basin, checks and corrects the data, divides the basin into 813 small grid squares, and uses statistical methods to identify changes in rainfall, temperature and other climate conditions. It also compares different datasets, checks the effects of satellite changes in 2014, and tests the reliability of every result. Each climate claim receives one of five possible verdicts: Supported, No Detectable Change, Datasets Disagree, Uncertain, or Not Enough Data. This allows the system to show when there is not enough evidence instead of making unsupported conclusions. The public website presents the results through interactive maps, climate claim pages, visual stories, village searches, flood information, an event viewer and scientific explanations. One of the main findings is that although 44 out of 813 grid squares show a significant decrease in rainfall, only one passes all reliability checks, while two NASA rainfall datasets disagree about the direction of change. This suggests that much of the apparent drying trend may be unreliable. However, autumn warming of 0.19°C per decade since 1980 is supported by all reliability checks. The project also compares rainfall and river discharge data with 1,028 reported flood incidents. Since heavy rainfall preceded only 12% of reported flood days and river discharge preceded 24%, the system does not provide its own flood forecasts or warnings. Another important feature, called “Where We Are Blind,” identifies areas with many reported floods but limited scientific evidence, helping show where additional rainfall and river monitoring stations may be needed. HimaRakshak AI is useful for journalists, government planners, researchers, teachers, students and local communities who want to understand climate changes using reliable information. People can search for their own villages, explore climate trends and trace every result back to its original data source and processing steps. The project uses Python, Pandas, NumPy, Xarray, SciPy, GeoPandas, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet and Plotly. It also includes a small Python MCP server with nine read-only tools, 102 automated tests and a reproducible pipeline that can run on an ordinary laptop without a GPU or cloud computing. What makes the project creative is its claim-as-a-case approach, where visitors first examine a chart and decide whether the climate has changed before seeing the scientific evidence and final verdict. They can also change the selected years to see how the results become stronger or weaker over time. The project follows important principles such as never fabricating data, showing negative results, keeping uncertain findings visible, fixing statistical rules before analysis and being transparent about methods and limitations. Overall, HimaRakshak AI is more than a climate mapping website; it is a transparent and evidence-based climate claim-checking system that helps people understand what is changing, what is uncertain and what cannot yet be proven about climate change in Nepal’s Koshi River Basin.
